articles.title: The Seed That Waited
articles.dek: In the 1960s, archaeologists pulled a few date pits out of the ruins at Masada. Forty years later one of them sprouted, and it helps explain what Peter meant by a seed that cannot die.
articles.quote: A word God plants in you can lie quiet for years, but it never dies, and it is only waiting for water.
articles.body:
In the mid-1960s, volunteers digging through the ruins of Herod's fortress at Masada, high on a cliff above the Dead Sea, picked a handful of small brown seeds out of the rubble. They were date pits, the kind a child spits onto the ground after a snack. The archaeologist Yigael Yadin's team catalogued them and packed them away. For the next forty years they sat in a drawer at Bar-Ilan University, forgotten like an old receipt in a wallet.

In 2005 Dr. Sarah Sallon, a physician who studied ancient medicinal plants, began to wonder whether anything might still be alive inside them. She took three of the seeds to Elaine Solowey, a plant scientist at Kibbutz Ketura in the Negev desert. Solowey later admitted that she expected nothing. She soaked the seeds in warm water, gave them a nutrient and hormone treatment, and pressed them into fresh soil. About eight weeks later, one of them cracked its shell and sent up a small green shoot.

Radiocarbon tests on fragments of that shell put the seed at roughly two thousand years old. The life inside it had been sealed away since about the time Jesus was walking the roads of Galilee. The team named the seedling Methuselah, after the oldest man in the Bible. It grew into a tall palm of the Judean variety that had disappeared from the land centuries earlier, and in later years the researchers woke more ancient seeds. One of them, a female palm they named Hannah, has since borne dates. Most of us think of a seed as small and fragile. Botanists know it as a sealed capsule of life, built to wait, and some seeds can wait far longer than anyone remembers planting them.

The apostle Peter never saw Methuselah sprout, but he understood seeds that wait. Around the early 60s AD he wrote a letter to scattered Christians across five Roman provinces in what is now Turkey (1 Peter 1:1). Picture one of those small gatherings in a house in Cappadocia: a few tradesmen, some household slaves, a widow or two, sitting close together while someone reads Peter's words aloud by lamplight. They had lost standing with their neighbors for following Jesus. Peter calls them foreigners (1 Peter 1:17), from the Greek paroikia, the word for a resident alien, someone who lives in a town without the rights of a citizen. They felt the way many overseas Filipinos feel: present every day, yet never quite at home.

Peter reminds them first of what their freedom cost. "For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life handed down to you from your ancestors, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or defect" (1 Peter 1:18–19). The word redeemed (lytroō) comes from the slave market, where a ransom price was paid to buy someone's freedom. The slaves listening in that room knew exactly how much silver it took to buy a person. Peter tells them their freedom was bought with something that will never lose its value.

Then he turns to how their new life began, and here he reaches for the picture of a seed.

"For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God. For, 'All people are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord endures forever.' And this is the word that was preached to you." (1 Peter 1:23–25)

The man who wrote those lines had once withered like grass in a single night. In a courtyard in Jerusalem, warming his hands at a charcoal fire, Peter swore three times that he had never known Jesus, and then he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:54–62). But a few hours before that collapse, Jesus had planted a word in him: "But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32). That sentence stayed buried inside Peter through the denial, through the crucifixion, and through the empty days afterward. Then, by another charcoal fire on the shore of Galilee, the risen Jesus asked him three times, "Do you love me?" and gave him back his calling (John 21:9, 15–17).

One way to read this letter is as that buried word finally sprouting. A frightened fisherman who once could not admit he knew Jesus in front of a servant girl is now writing to strangers across an empire to strengthen them. The very thing Jesus spoke over him came true years later.

Peter's own language deepens the picture. The word for seed is spora, the ordinary term for something sown. The word for imperishable is aphthartos, which means beyond the reach of decay. Peter has already used it in this chapter to describe the inheritance kept in heaven for believers (1 Peter 1:4). Even Methuselah's seed was perishable in the end. Most of the Masada pits never woke, and given enough time every earthly seed dies. Peter is describing a different kind of seed altogether, one with God's own life inside it, which time cannot wear out.

His quotation comes from Isaiah 40:6–8, words first spoken to Jewish exiles in Babylon who believed God had forgotten them. Peter hands the same promise to a new generation of exiles. Empires fade, reputations fade, and even our own strength fades like flowers in the Philippine dry season, but what God has said keeps its life. Jesus said the same thing: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away" (Matthew 24:35).

Peter draws a practical conclusion from all this, and it comes just before the seed passage: "love one another deeply, from the heart" (1 Peter 1:22). The word translated deeply is ektenōs, meaning stretched out or straining forward. Luke uses a related word for the church in Jerusalem, which was "earnestly praying" for Peter when Herod had him in chains (Acts 12:5). Peter knew what it felt like to be loved with that kind of stretched-out love. Because the life inside us comes from an imperishable seed, we can love others without fear of running dry.

This truth is a deep comfort for anyone carrying a long, quiet grief over someone they love. Perhaps a son once sang in the children's choir and now wants nothing to do with church. Perhaps a husband heard the gospel at a youth camp decades ago and has not opened a Bible since. Perhaps you are the one in a dry season, and the verses you memorized as a child feel like seeds sealed away in an old drawer. Peter's promise is that the word of God is "living and enduring" (1 Peter 1:23). It has not decayed in the dark. A word God plants in you can lie quiet for years, but it never dies, and it is only waiting for water.

Today you might bring to mind one verse that someone planted in you long ago, perhaps from a Lola, a Sunday school teacher, or a pastor whose name you have forgotten, and write it somewhere you will see it this week. Then think of one person in whom you know the word was once sown, and water it with a little stretched-out love: a prayer offered by name, a kind message, a meal shared without a sermon attached. You will not always see the shoot break through the soil, and Elaine Solowey waited weeks before she saw hers.

Methuselah is still growing in the desert at Ketura, a living reminder that life can outlast the drawer it was forgotten in. The word that was preached to you is stronger than that seed, because it carries the life of the God who raised Jesus from the dead (1 Peter 1:21). Your faith and your hope can rest there, and so can your hope for the people you love.

articles.title: The Cord Anyone Could Pull
articles.dek: God made Ezekiel a watchman for a tired, exiled people. The trumpet he blew came from a God who wanted them to live.
articles.quote: A warning spoken in love is the sound of someone who wants you to live.
articles.body:
In 1982, General Motors closed its assembly plant in Fremont, California. By many accounts it was one of the worst in the company. On some mornings so many workers stayed home that the line could barely start, grievances piled up by the thousands, and cars rolled out with defects that people on the floor had seen and kept quiet about. Two years later the plant reopened under an unlikely partnership. Toyota and GM formed a joint venture called NUMMI, and to the surprise of almost everyone, Toyota hired back much of the same workforce, including many of the old union leaders.

Groups of these workers were then sent to Japan to learn how Toyota built cars. One of the first things they met there was a simple rope running along the line, called the andon cord. Any worker who spotted a problem was expected to pull it. A team leader would come at once to help, and if the problem could not be fixed quickly, the whole line stopped. At the old Fremont plant, stopping the line was close to unthinkable, and a worker who did it could expect trouble. At Toyota, the person who pulled the cord was thanked. John Shook, an American who worked for Toyota and helped train the NUMMI teams, later wrote that the culture changed because people were given a way to raise an alarm and were treated as allies when they used it. Within a short time, the same workers who had been written off were building cars whose quality came close to Toyota's plants in Japan, and absenteeism dropped sharply.

Every family, church, and workplace has some kind of andon cord, whether it hangs in plain sight or stays hidden. What matters is whether anyone dares to pull it, and how they are received when they do. Ezekiel 33 takes up that very question, and God is the one asking it.

Ezekiel was a priest who was carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with the first wave of captives from Judah. He lived among the exiles by the Kebar River, preaching to homesick people who still hoped Jerusalem would somehow hold out. Chapter 32 closes a long section of prophecies against the surrounding nations with a haunting picture: proud Egypt going down into the pit, the realm of the dead, to lie among Assyria, Elam, and the other empires that once spread terror across the earth. It reads like a tour of a graveyard for superpowers. Then, in chapter 33, the camera swings back from the empires to the small, weary community sitting in front of Ezekiel, and God gives his prophet his job description again.

He uses an image every ancient listener understood. Cities had walls, and walls had towers, and in the towers stood a watchman scanning the horizon. When he saw an army coming, he blew the trumpet, usually a shofar, the ram's horn. The Hebrew word for watchman, tsofeh, comes from a verb that means to look out, to keep close watch. If the watchman sounded the alarm and the people ignored it, the fault was theirs. If he saw the sword coming and kept silent, God said, "I will hold the watchman accountable for their blood" (Ezek 33:6). Then God made it personal: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the people of Israel; so hear the word I speak and give them warning from me" (Ezek 33:7).

Taken alone, those verses can sound severe, even frightening. But God sets them right beside the exiles' own words of despair. They had finally stopped pretending. "Our offenses and sins weigh us down, and we are wasting away because of them. How then can we live?" (Ezek 33:10). God's answer to that cry is the heart of the whole chapter.

"Say to them, 'As surely as I live, declares the Sovereign LORD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn from their ways and live. Turn! Turn from your evil ways! Why will you die, people of Israel?'" (Ezek 33:11)

This verse explains why the watchman exists at all. God compares two outcomes, the death of the wicked and their turning, and he tells his people plainly which one he longs for. The trumpet is his way of keeping the door open. The Hebrew word behind "turn" is shuv, the ordinary word for coming back home after a journey, and God repeats it twice in a row, the way a parent calls a child back from a busy road. The question at the end, "Why will you die?", carries the sound of a grieving father more than an angry judge. One way to read the whole passage is that the warning and the welcome come from the same heart. The God who sends the watchman is like the team leader who comes running the moment the cord is pulled, eager to help fix what is broken so the work of living can go on.

The chapter also contains a gentle sting. A few verses later God tells Ezekiel that the people loved to hear him: "to them you are nothing more than one who sings love songs with a beautiful voice and plays an instrument well, for they hear your words but do not put them into practice" (Ezek 33:32). Something similar happened with NUMMI. For years, managers from across General Motors toured the Fremont plant, admired what they saw, and went home, yet much of the company struggled to bring the lesson back with them. They had seen the rope; what they found hard to copy was the trust that made people willing to pull it and willing to listen.

For many Filipinos, this passage touches a tender place. We value pakikisama, getting along, and we carry a deep sense of hiya, the shame of causing someone to lose face. Those instincts make us gracious, and they can also make us silent. We see a friend sliding into debt, a sibling drifting from God, a coworker cutting corners that will hurt him later, and we say nothing because speaking feels rude. Ezekiel reminds us that silence can be its own kind of unkindness. Proverbs says it simply: "Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses" (Prov 27:6). The New Testament gives the same charge to ordinary believers: "encourage one another daily, as long as it is called 'Today,' so that none of you may be hardened by sin's deceitfulness" (Heb 3:13).

The way God speaks in verse 11 shows us how to do it. His warning carries no contempt, only longing. If you need to speak to someone you love, let your words come from that same place: privately, humbly, with the person's good as your whole aim, and with a clear way home offered alongside the hard truth. A warning spoken in love is the sound of someone who wants you to live. And when you are the one being warned, receive it the way Toyota received the worker at the cord. Thank the person, even if your pride stings, because they have just done something costly for your sake.

Perhaps there is someone you have been meaning to talk to for months, and you have been waiting for a perfect moment that never seems to come. You might pray about it this morning and ask God for the right words and a gentle tone, then reach out this week over coffee or a quiet message. Or perhaps someone once cared enough to warn you, and their words changed the course of your life. Send them a note today and tell them you are grateful they pulled the cord.

The exiles thought their story had ended with the question "How then can we live?" God answered with an invitation to come home, and he still sends watchmen for the same reason. Every honest warning you give in love, and every one you receive with humility, becomes part of how he keeps calling his children back to life.

articles.title: The One Who Keeps the Night Watch
articles.dek: Psalm 121 was sung by weary pilgrims on the dangerous road to Jerusalem. Its quiet promise is that Someone stays awake through the dark, so that you can rest.
articles.quote: Because the One who keeps you never sleeps, you are free to close your eyes.
articles.body:
On the night of July 2, 2018, two British cave divers, John Volanthen and Rick Stanton, surfaced in a flooded chamber deep inside Tham Luang cave in northern Thailand. Their flashlights found thirteen thin faces on a muddy ledge: twelve boys from a local football team called the Wild Boars and their young coach, who had been missing for nine days. Volanthen's helmet camera was running, and the world later heard his gentle voice in the dark. He counted them, told them they were very strong, and gave them the news they had been waiting for. "Many people are coming," he said. "We are the first."

What happened next is the part of the story I love most. The following day, Thai Navy SEALs swam in with food and medicine, and with them came an army doctor, Lieutenant Commander Pak Loharnshoon. Pak and three SEALs stayed on that ledge with the boys for about a week while the rescue was planned and the water outside rose and fell. They told stories, checked pulses, and kept frightened children calm. The boys slept in the dark because someone beside them was awake. When the last of the boys was carried out on July 10, the doctor and his three companions were the final people to leave the cave. A brave former SEAL, Saman Kunan, gave his life during the operation, and Thailand honors him still. But for the boys, the memory that endured was simple: through every long night, someone kept watch.

I think of that ledge whenever I read Psalm 121. It is one of fifteen psalms (Psalms 120 to 134) titled "A song of ascents." Many scholars believe these were sung by pilgrims climbing toward Jerusalem for the great festivals, which every Israelite man was called to attend three times a year (Deuteronomy 16:16). The road was hard. It wound through the Judean hills, where travelers faced loose stones underfoot, a fierce sun by day, cold nights under open sky, and the occasional band of robbers waiting in the ravines. The psalm just before this one ends with a tired sigh from someone living among hostile neighbors: "I am for peace; but when I speak, they are for war" (Psalm 120:7). So Psalm 121 opens with a person who has decided to set out anyway.

"I lift up my eyes to the mountains, where does my help come from?" (Psalm 121:1). Readers have heard that line in two ways. Some hear comfort, as if the hills themselves were a source of strength. Many others hear an honest question, because those same hills held the dangers of the road, and on their summits stood the shrines where Israel's neighbors worshiped gods of rain and harvest. Either way, the pilgrim looks up at the heights and asks where help will really come from. The answer arrives at once: "My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:2). The traveler is trusting the One who made the mountains, which is a far steadier place to put one's hope than in the mountains themselves.

Then something lovely happens in the psalm, and it is easy to miss. The first two verses speak in the first person, with "I" and "my." From verse 3 onward, the voice changes to "you." One way to read this is as a conversation on the road. The pilgrim confesses his faith, and someone answers him, perhaps a fellow traveler at the campfire, a priest at the city gate, or a father blessing a son before the journey. Whoever is speaking, the words land like a hand on the shoulder:

"He will not let your foot slip, he who watches over you will not slumber; indeed, he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep." (Psalm 121:3–4)

The Hebrew word behind "watches over" is shamar, and it is the heartbeat of this psalm. In just eight verses it appears six times, translated as "watches over" and "keep." It is the word used when God placed Adam in the garden "to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15), and it describes a shepherd guarding a flock or a sentry standing on a city wall through the night. It is a working word for someone on duty. The psalm takes that ordinary picture of a night guard and applies it, again and again, to God himself.

The words "slumber" and "sleep" carry their own history. In the ancient world, people often imagined their gods as needing rest, and some myths described gods sleeping or growing drowsy. When Elijah faced the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, he teased them as their god stayed silent: "Maybe he is sleeping and must be awakened" (1 Kings 18:27). A pilgrim walking past hilltop shrines would have understood the point of Psalm 121 instantly. The God of Israel never needs to be roused. He never drifts off at his post, and he never wakes up late to find that something has happened while he rested.

Here is what moves me most. The psalm promises that God will not sleep, yet it never asks the traveler to stay awake. The pilgrim is allowed to lie down by the roadside, pull a cloak around his shoulders, and rest, because the watch has already been taken by Someone else. Another of the songs of ascents says the same thing plainly: "In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for food to eat, for he grants sleep to those he loves" (Psalm 127:2). David wrote it too, while running from his own son: "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, because the LORD sustains me" (Psalm 3:5). Because the One who keeps you never sleeps, you are free to close your eyes.

The rest of the psalm widens the circle of that care. "The LORD is your shade at your right hand" (Psalm 121:5) uses the language of a protector, since in the ancient world a defender or advocate stood at a person's right side (see Psalm 109:31). Any Filipino who has waited for a jeepney under the noon sun of April knows what shade is worth. "The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night" (Psalm 121:6) pairs the dangers people feared most, the burning of the day and the unknown terrors of the dark, and covers every hour between them. Finally, "the LORD will watch over your coming and going both now and forevermore" (Psalm 121:8) gathers up the whole of a life: every departure and every return, this year and every year after.

Many of us live as our own night watchmen. A mother sits up with a feverish child and cannot stop checking the thermometer. A seafarer or a nurse abroad lies awake in a dormitory thousands of kilometers from home, wondering whether the children are safe and whether the money sent last week was enough. A student lies in the dark before the board exam, replaying every formula. Some of us carry a long list of worries to bed every night and turn it over until two in the morning, as though our wakefulness could hold the world together. Psalm 121 gently tells us that the post we are guarding has already been filled.

Tonight, before you sleep, you might pray verses 3 and 4 aloud and then name, one by one, the people and problems that usually keep you awake, handing each of them over to the One who will neither slumber nor sleep. If you are sending someone off this week, at the airport, the bus terminal, or the front gate, you could bless them with verse 8 the way a parent once blessed a pilgrim, and trust that God watches both the leaving and the coming home.

In that Thai cave, the first voice in the dark told the boys that many people were coming, and then a doctor stayed with them until the very last child was safe. God's keeping goes deeper still. He is with you on the ledge and on the road, and he will still be awake long after the last light goes out tonight. You can lie down in peace, because he is keeping the watch.

articles.title: The Program That Let It Go
articles.dek: In a famous computer tournament, the strategy that thrived in a messy world was the one that could forgive. A Hebrew sage saw it first, and the cross showed it best.
articles.quote: Letting go of revenge means placing the account in the hands of the only Judge who keeps perfect books.
articles.illustration: Axelrod's tournament and Generous Tit for Tat
articles.body:
In 1980, Robert Axelrod, a political scientist at the University of Michigan, sent out an unusual invitation. He asked experts in game theory, the mathematics of how people make decisions, to submit computer programs that would play a simple game against one another, hundreds of rounds at a time. In each round a program could either cooperate or betray. If both cooperated, both earned points; if one betrayed while the other trusted, the betrayer won big and the trusting one got nothing; if both betrayed, both came away poor. The puzzle, known as the Prisoner's Dilemma, has fascinated economists and biologists for decades because it mirrors ordinary life, where cooperation helps everyone and betrayal still tempts each one of us.

Some of the entries were long and cunning. The winner was among the simplest submitted, a program written by the mathematician Anatol Rapoport called Tit for Tat. It began by cooperating and then simply copied whatever its opponent had done the round before. Axelrod held a second tournament with dozens more entries, and Tit for Tat won again. His 1984 book, The Evolution of Cooperation, became a classic, and its lesson seemed settled: be kind first, and always pay back in kind.

Then researchers added something those first tournaments lacked, which was ordinary error. In real life, signals get crossed, a friendly move is misread as hostile, and a message arrives garbled. Under those conditions Tit for Tat stumbled badly, because one accidental slight set off an echo that never ended. You hit me, so I hit you, so you hit me again, and two decent programs stayed locked in a feud that neither had started on purpose. In 1992, the mathematical biologists Martin Nowak and Karl Sigmund reported in the journal Nature that a gentler strategy did far better in that noisy world. They called it Generous Tit for Tat, and it behaved like the original with one change: some of the time, when it was wronged, it let the wrong go and cooperated anyway. That small habit of forgiveness broke the cycles of revenge, and the generous program came out ahead.

Nearly three thousand years earlier, a Hebrew sage wrote the same discovery into one sentence. It sits in a short collection that begins at Proverbs 24:23 with the words "These also are sayings of the wise," compact lessons for young people learning to live well in Israel's villages. Those were small places where families shared wells and boundary stones, and where disputes were settled in public at the city gate. Life there was a long, repeated game with the same neighbors, year after year, harvest after harvest.

Verse 28 warns, "Do not testify against your neighbor without cause" (Proverbs 24:28). The Hebrew word behind "without cause" is chinnam, which means gratuitously, for nothing, with no real reason. Then verse 29 exposes the motive that might drive a person to the gate with an exaggerated charge. Picture a farmer whose neighbor spoke against him last season, or quietly shifted a boundary stone. Now that neighbor is in trouble, the elders are gathering, and the farmer feels the old wound stir as he rehearses the words in his head.

"Do not say, 'I'll do to them as they have done to me; I'll pay them back for what they did.'" (Proverbs 24:29)

The first half of that sentence is the Golden Rule turned inside out. Jesus would later teach, "Do to others what you would have them do to you" (Matthew 7:12). The voice in Proverbs 24:29 runs the rule backward and says to do to others what they did to you. It is Tit for Tat in plain words, and it sounds perfectly fair, which is exactly why it is so persuasive.

The second half holds a detail that opens the whole verse. The Hebrew phrase translated "I'll pay them back for what they did" uses the verb shuv, to return, and the noun po'al, a deed; woodenly, it reads "I will return to the man according to his work." Seventeen verses earlier, the same chapter uses those very words about God: "Will he not repay everyone according to what they have done?" (Proverbs 24:12). The sage placed the two lines within the same few paragraphs. Repayment according to deeds is real in God's universe, and the only question is who holds that office. Verse 12 gives it to the Lord, and verse 29 describes the moment a person reaches over and tries to take it for himself. Proverbs says it again elsewhere: "Do not say, 'I'll pay you back for this wrong!' Wait for the LORD, and he will avenge you" (Proverbs 20:22).

Axelrod's noisy tournaments help explain why God keeps that office. We live in a world full of static. We misread tone, we guess at motives, and we remember our own side of the story with remarkable clarity and the other side with remarkable vagueness. Our record of the wrong is precisely the kind of signal that gets garbled. God sees every heart without distortion, so he alone can repay without error, and leaving the matter with him is the wisest thing a limited person can do.

Scripture goes deeper than strategy, though. The strongest reason to put down the ledger is that God himself declined to play Tit for Tat with us. "He does not treat us as our sins deserve or repay us according to our iniquities" (Psalm 103:10). Every one of us has betrayed God, round after round, and he answered with the cross. Of Jesus, Peter writes, "When they hurled their insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he entrusted himself to him who judges justly" (1 Peter 2:23). Justice was satisfied in full at Calvary, carried by Jesus himself, so that mercy could reach people like us. The gospel is the most generous move ever made, and it is the reason Paul can urge believers, "Do not repay anyone evil for evil" (Romans 12:17).

Filipinos know the pull of the backward rule well. We have words for it, from the old gantihan to the younger resbak, and many families carry a quarrel over a piece of land in the province that has outlived the people who began it. On a smaller scale, the same echo plays out when one sharp comment in a group chat draws a sharper reply, and by evening two cousins have stopped speaking. Very often the first offense was noise: a tired relative, a text read in the wrong tone, a joke that landed badly.

Forgiveness of this kind is different from pretending nothing happened. Generous Tit for Tat still responded honestly to its opponent, and Proverbs 24 is addressing personal revenge, so real harm such as abuse or fraud should still be brought to those with rightful authority to deal with it. What the verse asks is that you stop appointing yourself the one who settles the score. When the next wrong comes, you might give the other person one extra round of goodwill before you conclude the worst, and then name the hurt plainly to God in prayer, telling him what was done and leaving the repayment in his hands.

Nowak's generous program did not forgive perfectly, and neither will you. Each time you choose it, though, you break an echo that might otherwise have run for years, and you give someone else room to return to cooperation. You also get to live lighter, because the debt you used to carry now rests with Someone stronger. Letting go of revenge means placing the account in the hands of the only Judge who keeps perfect books, and that Judge is the same Father who looked at your own long record and chose, at great cost to himself, to let it go.
